Every claim checks out against the letter: Henry's first letter home, the 34th New York's arrival at Washington via Baltimore, the twenty men detailed with loaded guns "in case of attack," the city's tepid "rather cheered" reception, the bullet holes in the depot roof from an earlier disturbance, the declined furlough on cost grounds, and the eight dollars sent home to his widowed mother. The "earlier row" framing for the bullet holes is a reasonable period-faithful reading.

FEEDBACK: This is a strong, well-grounded draft that earns its length and stays vivid. It nails the historical hook — a brand-new regiment's first passage through Baltimore, the very city where the 6th Massachusetts had been mobbed and bloodied that April, which is exactly why twenty men marched with loaded weapons and why the depot still bore bullet holes. The summary lets a knowing reader feel that tension without importing the outside event (per the no-outside-events rule), and the "rather cheered" detail is a lovely, precise period note that complicates the expected hostility. The human beat — declining the furlough so his mother keeps the eight dollars — lands naturally and is woven, not tacked on. Minor calibration: "an earlier row" slightly undersells; the letter's own language and the loaded-gun detail signal real, recent danger, so a word like "earlier trouble" or "earlier clash" carries the menace a hair better without spoiling or importing. The phrase "Already mindful of his widowed mother" is a touch editorial-explanatory; the act itself already shows the mindfulness. Both are polish, not problems.

old: Henry is writing from Washington while hearing the cannons of the First Battle of Bull Run (Manassas) — the first major battle of the Civil War, fought July 21, 1861, approximately 25-30 miles from Washington. This is a real-time eyewitness account of the battle's sound reaching the capital.
draft: Writing from Washington on July 21, 1861, Henry tells his mother that "while I am writing there is a battle going on," with cannons firing "not over twenty-eight miles from here" — a real-time eyewitness account of distant fighting. Uncertain whether his regiment will move or serve as city guard, he steadies himself in faith hours after a six o'clock chapel service, adding that wherever he goes, he is ready.

FEEDBACK: The summary is accurate, period-correct, and well-chosen in its anchors. The 1861 Potomac picket-guard posting, the green-regiment anxiety about "never seeing a battle," and the camp-accident death are exactly the historically significant beats — they situate this firmly in the static, disease-and-drill first autumn of the war before the regiment ever faced combat, which a historian tracing the collection's arc needs. The three-quote density is the one real weakness: three direct quotations in 350-odd characters reads slightly as a quote-reel, and the gold-piece "command" line, while charming, is the least historically load-bearing. Two smaller notes: "rebel crossings" is period-apt phrasing and fine; and the letter's quiet undercurrent — Henry sick, unable to drill three days, in a camp that is "a great place for fever and ague" — is the human/historical beat actually most emblematic of 1861 camp life, and the draft omits it entirely in favor of the eager-for-battle line. That illness detail would deepen the period texture more than the gold-piece command. Consider trimming one quote and threading in the sickness to better balance the soldier's bravado against the real killer of his war.

critiques.text:
FACT ISSUES: none. Every claim is grounded in the letter: the correction of the report ("not three Comp. of Rebels, but only thirty-five against twelve"), the rheumatism he blames on conditions and treats with the floor ("I should probably have the rheumatism now if we had not got the floor"), the 95-cent tent floor, the colonel's card ban ("There was to much gambling going on"), and the spelling joke ("I could not spell the word"). One small nuance: the letter says they "got a floor" to the tent — "tent floor" is faithful, and the 95 cents is exact. The draft's "splurged" is a light editorial gloss but defensible given the 30-cents-apiece arithmetic he works out. The "attack over the river" is rendered as "an attack across the river," which is accurate.

FEEDBACK: This is strong and period-faithful. The anchor is well chosen — the corrected war report is the historically significant beat (it's a soldier acting as a check on civilian rumor, "I wonder you did not hear there was a thousand"), and the rheumatism-and-floor sequence captures the real medical economy of camp life that the editorial note flags. The human beat (the spelling joke) lands and is woven, not tacked on. Two refinements worth making: first, "an attack across the river" is slightly vague — in late September 1861 near Washington this is the Potomac picket line, and even without naming outside events you can lean on the period texture of rumor inflation, which is the letter's real point. Second, the draft is a four-clause pile-up in two long sentences; it reads as a list joined by dashes and "He notes." The card ban and the spelling joke are both good but compete; consider subordinating one. Length (~480 chars) runs slightly over the 350-450 target. Tightening also sharpens the voice.

SUGGESTED: Writing to his brother Charles, Henry plays fact-checker on a rumor that reached home: the "attack over the river" was no three companies of Rebels but thirty-five men against twelve — "I wonder you did not hear there was a thousand." He recounts a hard bout of rheumatism, blamed on sleeping on bare ground and eased only after he and his tentmates spent 95 cents on a floor, and notes the colonel's fresh ban on card-playing after too much gambling. He owns up that he'd put off writing of the illness because he couldn't spell the word.

FACT ISSUES: none. The unit context (Henry, Co. D, 34th NY) aligns with the collection; the letter's internal military facts — "Camp in field," heavy musketry toward Yorktown, the double-quick of about a mile two days prior, the diary of 28 dated entries — are all reportable from this letter. The draft does not import the actual April 1862 Yorktown siege chronology or any outside engagement, which is correct.

FEEDBACK: Militarily the draft is sound and well-emphasized. The Yorktown setting is exactly right for the 34th NY in early April 1862 (Peninsula Campaign, advance on the Confederate Warwick–Yorktown line), and the draft correctly treats the musketry and the double-quick alarm as the kind of expectant-but-no-battle tension that defined the siege approach rather than overclaiming a fight. One sharpening: "most of Co. D held together" is a slightly soft, ambiguous phrase for a military reader — if the letter is contrasting men who fell out or straggled on the double-quick versus those who kept ranks, say that more concretely; if Henry's point is steadiness under a false alarm, name it as such. Also "double-quicked a mile expecting a fight" is good and concrete — keep it. The diary detail is a strong human/archival beat and earns its place. Watch that the close ("mind the cows and horse, hoping to be home next summer") doesn't crowd the West Point thread; both are domestic-future notes and together they slightly dilute the military center. The draft is within length and vivid.

SUGGESTED: From "Camp in field" with heavy musketry sounding off toward Yorktown, Henry writes his brother James that he has kept a pocket diary — 28 dated entries recording "everything that transpires from day to day." Two days before, Co. D was double-quicked nearly a mile expecting a fight that never came, most of the company holding its ranks. Even amid the siege lines he presses James toward West Point, asks him to mind the cows and horse, and lets himself hope to be home next summer.
